analysis.one_liner: Bars companies from forcing data-breach victims into arbitration instead of court.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or a vote; it sat in the House Energy and Commerce Committee and its Consumer Protection Subcommittee until the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: When a company's customer data gets breached, the fine print customers signed often forces them into private arbitration — a process with no judge, no jury, and usually no class action — instead of court. This bill would have banned that: companies could not require arbitration for disputes over a security breach, existing clauses would be void, victims could sue for damages with attorney's fees paid, and the FTC and state attorneys general could enforce the ban. It never moved beyond a subcommittee referral and died when the 117th Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers whose sensitive personal information is exposed in a data breach. Today, if a company loses your Social Security number or card data, the agreement you signed may force your dispute into arbitration — where you proceed alone, with no class action to aggregate small claims, and often with confidential proceedings. The bill would let breach victims go to court, recover attorney's fees so a claim is worth bringing, and would apply to clauses already in force by voiding them. Law firms handling consumer class actions, and the FTC and state attorneys general as enforcers, would also gain a new tool.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Victims of data breaches and identity theft

how_it_helps.text: It bars companies from forcing customers into arbitration over disputes tied to a security breach, including identity theft, and voids any existing agreement clause that violates that rule

It creates a private right of action letting breach victims sue for damages, restitution, and injunctions, with attorney's fees, expert witness fees, and litigation costs recoverable — which makes it financially practical for an individual to bring a case
It adds two public enforcers: the Federal Trade Commission can treat violations as unfair or deceptive practices, and state attorneys general can sue on behalf of their residents
The clock for suing runs for two years from the violation or two years from when it was discovered, whichever is later, so victims who learn of a breach late are not barred from court

analysis.who_pays: Companies that hold consumer data — retailers, banks, credit bureaus, tech platforms — would face a new route to court and potentially large class claims after breaches, plus FTC and state enforcement. Their executives and directors could face personal liability for violations. Some of that cost would show up in prices and security spending, but the bill's premise is that breach costs should fall on the companies that failed to prevent them rather than on the people whose data was stolen.

drawbacks.text: The private right of action imposes joint and several liability on individual executives, directors, partners, and employees who 'materially aid' a violation, which is an unusually broad personal-liability exposure that critics would call excessive

The bill lets suits proceed over any unauthorized acquisition or access of 'sensitive personally identifiable information,' a definition broad enough to sweep in data elements like names combined with addresses, which could produce litigation over breaches that caused little measurable harm

Companies with customer agreements would lose a tool they argue keeps dispute resolution faster and cheaper than court litigation, though arbitration's limits on class claims are exactly what the bill targets

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real: forced arbitration clauses routinely block consumers from banding together in class actions over data breaches, and individual claims are usually too small to litigate alone, so companies rarely pay for the harm their lapses cause. This bill would have opened the courthouse door for exactly those cases, added fee-shifting so ordinary victims could actually afford counsel, and given the FTC and state attorneys general a new enforcement tool. The honest costs are on the other side: treating a clause in a customer agreement as a personal liability trigger for executives and employees is unusually broad, and allowing suits over any breach of a broad data definition raises the risk of large claims over breaches that cause little actual harm — costs that would land in security spending and prices. On balance, the public interest in a workable remedy after a breach seems to outweigh those design concerns, but the bill died without a hearing or a vote, so it was never tested, debated, or refined.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Energy and Commerce Committee and its Consumer Protection Subcommittee the day after introduction, no one else signed on, and it never advanced before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Ted Lieu introduced the bill on May 17, 2021, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce
On May 18, 2021, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Consumer Protection and Commerce, where it remained
No member of either party signed on as a cosponsor at any point in the two-year Congress
The complete action history contains no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action; the last recorded action is the subcommittee referral of May 18, 2021

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Companies that hold consumer data keep the ability to enforce arbitration clauses against breach victims, so their interests are unchanged; nobody else gained anything from the bill's death.

for.name: Rep. Ted Lieu
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and was its only sponsor; no colleague ever cosponsored it

against.name: Rep. Frank Pallone
against.role: Chair, House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Chaired the committee the bill was referred to; the record shows no hearing, markup, or committee vote was ever scheduled on it

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee and its Consumer Protection Subcommittee
against.what_they_did: Held the bill from May 2021 until the Congress ended in January 2023 without any further action

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken and no other member signed on from either party, so no partisan line ever formed on the bill.

industries.industry: Companies that hold consumer data (retailers, banks, tech platforms, credit bureaus)
industries.note: With the bill dead, they keep the ability to write arbitration clauses that channel data-breach disputes into a forum with no class actions and limited public records, which has the practical effect of limiting what breach victims recover.

industries.industry: Arbitration providers and the consumer-arbitration industry
industries.note: Forced arbitration survives for data-breach disputes, preserving a stream of disputes that would otherwise have moved to the courts.

industries.industry: Consumer-side class action and privacy litigation firms
industries.note: The bill would have created a new supply of fee-shifting cases over data breaches; none of that market materialized.
